story.headline: Fed Governor Christopher Waller backed a possible half-point US rate hike in December, keeping the dollar near a 19-month high. The Aussie fell to a 10-month low after Australia lost jobs in October.

reads.policy: Fed Governor Christopher Waller argued for a half-point US hike in December unless the Fed signals another in January, and bets on a bigger step doubled. Weak Australian jobs figures point the other way there, supporting the view that Australian rates have peaked. US rates still look set to rise fastest, which keeps favouring the dollar.
reads.growth: Australia lost jobs for a second month and unemployment hit a five-year high, the clearest sign yet that high rates are biting there. The US economy still looks firmer than most, which supports the dollar. Coming up: US weekly jobless claims.
reads.inflation: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Japan's inflation figures, out Thursday evening US time, will show whether the Bank of Japan has a clear case to hike in December.
reads.risk: A Houthi missile aimed at the Saudi capital caused damage overnight, yet markets stayed calm and the franc and yen drew no haven buying. With Gulf oil still flowing, interest rates are doing more to move currencies than the war. Weak Australian jobs added to pressure on the Aussie.
reads.tot: Oil steadied after a big drop as Gulf flows returned to normal, which keeps weighing on the Canadian dollar and helps energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area. Gold's slide to its lowest in more than a year weighs on the Aussie, since Australia is a big gold producer.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds leaning toward the dollar and the pound and against the euro, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar, with bets against the kiwi growing fastest. Big long-term investors take the other side on the euro, pound and Aussie. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs near 5%, which weighs a little on trust in the dollar.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Almost all officials now expect more hikes, and Governor Christopher Waller argues for a half-point step in December, which keeps the dollar near its highest since April 2025.
fed.priced: December: hike all but certain, with a half-point move a growing chance. More hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal. Waller says the Fed should go a half point in December unless it clearly signals another hike in January.
fed.watch: Weekly jobless claims Thursday, November 19 at 7:30 AM CT, and Waller again Friday, November 20 at 7:25 AM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Oil prices, which fell sharply this week, and Canada's November jobs figures on December 4. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi has fallen to its lowest since 2020.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Final figures confirmed euro-area inflation at 4.0% with core prices revised up, but the euro has slipped below $1.10 as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Weak factories and France's debts, which the bank's stability report singled out, limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: President Christine Lagarde speaks Thursday, November 19 at 7:30 AM CT and Friday, November 20 at 2:15 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Governor Kazuo Ueda says rates will keep rising and warns that the weak yen is lifting food prices.
boj.why: The weak yen is pushing import costs and food prices up, and record chip exports show the economy can take higher rates. The small summer contraction is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Japan's national inflation figures Thursday, November 19 at 5:30 PM CT, and whether Japan buys yen if the dollar tops 160. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Australia lost jobs in October and unemployment hit a five-year high, which supports the view that rates have peaked and weighs on the Aussie.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected. Some bets on cuts in 2027 are building.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high for most of the board, but the job market is clearly weakening. That makes a further hike unlikely and puts the timing of a first cut in question.
rba.watch: Any comment from Governor Michele Bullock on the jobs figures, and gold prices. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. Steady UK core inflation and Governor Andrew Bailey's caution have trimmed bets on a second hike in December, which is still seen as likely.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal. Bailey says the longer the war lasts, the higher rates must go, but the bank is not on a set path.
boe.watch: UK retail sales Friday, November 20 at 1:00 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight. It has still slipped to its lowest since mid-October as US rate bets climb faster.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Australia's October job losses suggest those rates have peaked, and the Aussie fell to its lowest in about 10 months.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High and rising US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh a little. Talk of a half-point Fed hike in December has kept it near its highest since April 2025.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm prices for New Zealand's dairy exports help, but doubts over a December rate hike have kept it near its lowest since 2020.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Cheaper oil helps the euro area, but France's debts and rates below most of the others hold it back. Faster US rate rises keep it just under $1.10.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. The US dollar is at its high for the year against it.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A likely December Bank of Japan hike and warnings from Japan's finance minister only just keep the dollar below 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. The dollar is at its highest against it in about 18 months.
